title: From Target Chemistry to AI-Assisted PD
bullets: Use what you know about target structure and chemical recognition.
Ask how AI helps choose molecules and the experiments that test them.
caption: Published AF3 complexes: different molecules require different recognition models.
notes: Connect to prior target classes without reteaching the pharmacology chapters. These are published predictions, not calculations made for this lesson.

title: Follow a Drug–Target Research Question
bullets: Define the interaction or effect before choosing a tool.
Move from a target to a testable chemical decision.
caption: Target → structure → candidates → experiments → next decision.

title: AI Tools for Pharmacodynamic Research
bullets: Choose by the question, the available data and the meaning of the output.
caption: Examples of useful research tools—not a popularity or performance ranking.
source: Official documentation and original tool papers; details in notes.
notes: Sources: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07487-w ; https://prankweb.cz/ ; https://github.com/gnina/gnina ; https://github.com/jwohlwend/boltz/blob/main/docs/prediction.md ; https://chemprop.readthedocs.io/ ; https://doi.org/10.1186/s13321-024-00812-5 . Tools differ in training needs, licensing and setup.

title: Use Disease Evidence to Prioritize Targets
bullets: Combine disease-related measurements with established biological knowledge.
AI ranking proposes a target; it does not validate the target.
caption: TNIK study: biological evidence used in target prioritization.
source: Ren et al., Nat. Biotechnol. 43, 63–75 (2025; online 2024).
notes: Input-evidence panel from the published workflow. Explain genes, proteins and disease associations, not the model architecture.

title: Enzymes: Start from a Real Binding Complex
bullets: Sildenafil–PDE5 provides a known inhibitor and a defined pocket.
Use that reference to prepare an AI-assisted screening question.
caption: Experimental sildenafil–PDE5 structure, PDB 1UDT.
notes: Sildenafil was not discovered by the AI methods taught here. This experimental reference is specific to the stated enzyme project.

title: Predict a Complex When a Structure Is Missing
bullets: Provide the identities of the interacting molecules.
Use predicted geometry as a starting hypothesis—not measured activity.
caption: AF3 examples include protein–RNA, antibody and small-molecule complexes.
notes: Published Figure 3. Blue/green: predicted proteins; orange: predicted ligands/glycans; purple: predicted RNA; grey: experimental comparison. Explain selected examples, not numerical structure metrics.

title: Find Candidate Pockets with P2Rank
bullets: A pocket predictor highlights regions that may bind a ligand.
Known chemistry and experiments help decide which site matters.
caption: Published DGAT2 pocket illustration; a candidate region is not a confirmed drug site.
notes: The panel concerns DGAT2 and predicted pocket features. P2Rank/PrankWeb proposes binding regions, not affinity or cellular efficacy.

title: GPCRs: Choose the Relevant Receptor State
bullets: Active and inactive receptors present different binding environments.
Choose the state relevant to the prediction and functional assay.
caption: β₂-adrenoceptor: inactive and active experimental structures; TM6 highlighted.
source: RCSB PDB 2RH1 and 3SN6; Rasmussen et al., Nature 477, 549–555 (2011).
notes: Inactive blue; active wheat/orange. The overlay is a comparison of experimental states, not a computed transition or thermodynamic ensemble.

title: Give the Tool the Correct Chemical Structure
bullets: Keep connectivity, charge and stereochemistry explicit.
Adrenaline illustrates why those chemical details cannot be ignored.
caption: R-adrenaline shown with a protonated secondary amine.
source: Original chemical illustration; molecular identity checked computationally.
notes: The input form is a teaching example. No numerical affinity or activity is assigned.

title: Docking: Propose and Test a Binding Pose
bullets: GNINA can rank proposed ligand arrangements with learned scoring.
Use this experimental EGFR complex as a reference—not a new prediction.
caption: Experimental erlotinib–EGFR reference, PDB 1M17; not a new GNINA result.
source: McNutt et al., J. Cheminform. 17, 28 (2025). RCSB PDB 1M17.
notes: This defined kinase–inhibitor complex explains what a pose is and what redocking would try to recover. Conventional sampling and AI scoring are different operations.

title: Use Chemical Contacts to Inspect a Prediction
bullets: Check whether polar and nonpolar groups face suitable regions.
A plausible contact pattern is not a measurement of binding strength.
caption: Rosuvastatin in the experimental HMG-CoA reductase complex, PDB 1HWL.
notes: The experimental statin complex is used as a chemically specific reference for inspecting model predictions. The drug is not described as AI-discovered.

title: Search Beyond the Usual Active Site
bullets: An allosteric ligand can act at a different pocket.
Specify the intended site when predicting or scoring binding.
caption: Experimental allosteric inhibitor complex of PI5P4Kγ, PDB 7QIE.
source: Abramson et al., Nature 630, 493–500 (2024). RCSB PDB 7QIE.
notes: The AF3 paper includes this allosteric-site example. This new rendering uses experimental coordinates; it is not the published AF3 prediction.

title: Boltz-2: Read the Right Output
bullets: Structural confidence, binding likelihood and activity estimates are different.
Validate the particular claim represented by each output.
caption: A confident-looking structure is not an experimental binding measurement.
source: Boltz-2 original paper and official prediction documentation (2025).
notes: Do not teach logarithmic score conversion. Do not rename predicted activity as experimental Kd. Model setup and its documented applicability matter.

title: Nuclear Receptors: A Pose Does Not Define Function
bullets: Oestradiol and raloxifene stabilize different receptor arrangements.
An AI binding pose still needs a matching receptor-response assay.
caption: Oestrogen receptor comparison: oestradiol blue; raloxifene wheat/orange.
notes: Helix 12 is highlighted. Raloxifene is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator with tissue-dependent effects, not a universal antagonist.

title: Covalent Inhibitors: Model the Bound Chemistry
bullets: Ampicillin forms a covalent acyl-enzyme complex with a PBP.
Use covalent-aware preparation; docking does not predict the reaction.
caption: Experimental covalent ampicillin–PBP4 complex, PDB 2EX6.
source: Kishida et al., Biochemistry 45, 783–792 (2006). McNutt et al., J. Cheminform. 17, 28 (2025).
notes: PBP4 is a cell-wall-remodelling DD-peptidase, not the bifunctional PBP1b. GNINA covalent docking requires the bound form; it does not predict the reaction. Its CNN was not trained on covalent complexes.

title: Ion Channels: Flag Possible hERG Blockers
bullets: HERGAI predicts hERG inhibition from molecule–channel information.
Use the prediction to prioritize electrophysiology tests.
caption: Experimental hERG channel structure, PDB 5VA1; no blocker pose is asserted.
source: Tran-Nguyen et al., J. Cheminform. 17, 110 (2025); PDB 5VA1.
notes: hERG is a potassium channel. A blocker prediction is not a probability of clinical arrhythmia. No architecture or threshold calculations are needed.

title: Screen Broadly; Test a Manageable Shortlist
bullets: AI-assisted ranking can reduce the number of compounds sent to the laboratory.
Keep chemically sensible and sufficiently diverse candidates.
caption: Illustrative candidate collection; no activities or model scores are assigned.
notes: The structures are distinct synthetic teaching candidates, not compounds from a claimed experiment.

title: Predict Activity from Measured Examples
bullets: Chemprop can learn a defined activity endpoint from appropriate assay data.
Test predictions on compounds not used to build the model.
caption: A structure and an assay result form a learning example.
source: Heid et al., J. Chem. Inf. Model. 64, 9–17 (2024).
notes: Only an input–output explanation is needed. Chemprop needs relevant data or a suitable existing model; it is not universally pretrained for every target.

title: Small Changes: Theophylline versus Caffeine
bullets: These molecules differ by one methyl group.
The RNA-recognition example shows why a model must distinguish them.
caption: A theophylline-binding RNA aptamer discriminates against caffeine.
source: Zimmermann et al., Nat. Struct. Biol. 4, 644–649 (1997).
notes: This is a documented molecular-recognition example, not a new AI prediction or a general rule about methylation.

title: RNA Targets Need RNA-Relevant Models
bullets: SMRTnet combines RNA sequence/secondary structure with the candidate molecule.
Protein-trained binding predictions should not be transferred to RNA without testing.
caption: Experimental theophylline–RNA aptamer, PDB 1EHT; one NMR model.
source: Fei et al., Nat. Biotechnol. (2026), doi:10.1038/s41587-025-02942-z. PDB 1EHT.
notes: The specific aptamer illustrates RNA recognition; SMRTnet studied theophylline-related discrimination. This rendering is experimental reference geometry, not a model output.

title: Ask AI to Propose New Chemical Ideas
bullets: REINVENT 4 can decorate a scaffold, link fragments or propose new molecules.
Design goals guide proposals; synthesis and assays determine their value.
caption: Four molecular-design tasks in REINVENT 4.
notes: Original Figure 4. Explain the chemical changes and fixed starting information; omit neural architectures and optimization equations.

title: Predict a Target Profile, Not Just One Score
bullets: Related proteins and unwanted targets may also interact with the molecule.
Follow promising predictions with an appropriate target panel.
caption: Hypothetical matched-assay inhibition patterns—not measured candidates.
notes: Some multi-target effects are useful. Selectivity is not sufficient to establish clinical safety.

title: DNA Targets Need a Relevant Binding Model
bullets: Intercalation and groove binding pose different recognition problems.
Use DNA-relevant inputs and binding tests—not assumed protein-model transfer.
caption: Experimental anthracycline–DNA complex, PDB 1D12.
notes: This extends the previous nucleic-acid course to model choice. No universal AI DNA-affinity tool or sequence selectivity is claimed.

title: Check Target Function with Experiments
bullets: A predicted binding arrangement needs independent experimental tests.
Enzyme and cellular assays test function—not equilibrium binding alone.
caption: Ren et al., Figure 2: predicted structures and distinct functional measurements.
source: Ren et al., Nat. Biotechnol. 43, 63–75 (2025; online 2024).
notes: Figure 2 does not provide the direct SPR binding evidence. The SPR experiment is Extended Data Figure 3a. The displayed data concern TNIK enzymatic inhibition and cellular functional readouts.

title: Use Cell Images to Measure the Response
bullets: Images capture changes in cell shape and internal organization.
AI-assisted image analysis needs controls and a clearly defined biological question.
caption: Published Cell Painting example; images are experimental inputs.
notes: Do not describe a fluorescence image as a direct binding assay or infer an unstated cell identity. Cell Painting and image segmentation are not equivalent to target identification.

title: Work Backwards from an Unexplained Cell Effect
bullets: Compare the compound’s profile with well-characterized references.
A similar pattern suggests a mechanism to test, not a proven shared target.
caption: Simulated profiles show how reference matching can generate a hypothesis.
notes: Transcriptomic and morphological profiles are complementary sources, not mandatory sequential stages. Distinguish shared stress from shared target action.

title: Let Experiments Change the Next Design
bullets: Use both successful and unsuccessful compounds to refine the next choice.
The best next experiment may test a new chemical idea, not the highest score.
caption: Design → make → test → learn: AI supports the experimental cycle.
notes: Do not introduce acquisition functions or claim that synthesis and biological validation have been automated in this teaching example.

title: Case 1: AI Helped Design TNIK Inhibitors
bullets: After target prioritization, Chemistry42 proposed candidate structures.
Synthesis and experimental filtering guided candidate selection.
caption: Published structure-based design inputs and filters—not a fully automated discovery.
source: Ren et al., Nat. Biotechnol. 43, 63–75 (2025; online 2024).
notes: The approximately eighteen-month milestone was preclinical candidate nomination, not first-in-human testing. It is not a controlled estimate of the time saved by AI.

title: Case 1: Separate Prediction from Measured PD
bullets: The candidate bound TNIK and inhibited the enzyme.
Cell assays showed fibrosis-related effects; those need mechanistic interpretation.
caption: Published cellular assay evidence for INS018_055.
source: Ren et al., Nat. Biotechnol. 43, 63–75 (2025; online 2024).
notes: Broader kinase activity prevents attributing every cellular effect exclusively to TNIK. A predicted pose is not an experimental co-crystal. No clinical approval is claimed.

title: Case 2: Expand a Fragment into New Candidates
bullets: The published fragment route starts from an antibacterial chemical clue.
Predicted activity and toxicity help choose compounds for synthesis.
caption: Published generative-antibiotic strategy; candidate generation precedes validation.
notes: Do not teach VAE, genetic-algorithm or graph-network details. Large computational candidate pools are not experimentally tested compounds.

title: Case 2: Test the Designed Antibiotics
bullets: The full study synthesized 24 compounds; seven were selectively antibacterial.
The displayed NG series links generated structures to antibacterial tests.
caption: Published antibacterial study: chemistry and experiments, not human efficacy.
notes: NG1 was investigated against Neisseria gonorrhoeae and DN1 against Staphylococcus aureus. Mechanistic follow-up is not direct proof of a resolved drug–target complex.

title: Case 3: Predict the Receptor, Then Screen Ligands
bullets: AlphaFold2 supplied receptor models; docking selected candidate molecules.
Experiments checked binding and followed up selected complexes.
caption: Experimental 5-HT₂A complex from the study’s structural follow-up, PDB 8UWL.
notes: The pictured structure is explicitly experimental follow-up. AI predicted the receptor; the screened molecules were not generated by AlphaFold2.

title: Case 3: Did Model-Based Screening Help?
bullets: Both predicted-structure and experimental-structure campaigns found binders.
Similar results in this comparison do not guarantee success on every target.
caption: Rounded published hit rates refer to compounds actually tested.
notes: The model-based sigma-2 campaign found 64 hits among 119 tested compounds. The roughly 54% versus 51% difference was not significant. Do not claim superiority.

title: Case 4: Use Chemical Clues to Select Antibiotics
bullets: Models learned from antibacterial activity and human-cell toxicity.
Highlighted substructures helped guide prospective compound selection.
caption: Published chemical rationales and candidate scaffolds.
notes: The source’s real chemical substructures replace unrelated teaching molecules. Explain a rationale as a model-associated chemical clue, not a proven biological mechanism.

title: Case 4: Laboratory Evidence Goes Beyond a Score
bullets: The study experimentally tested 283 selected compounds.
A discovered chemical class received mechanistic and mouse-infection studies.
caption: Published preclinical efficacy evidence; not a human clinical result.
notes: No claim that all 283 were active. Selected subgroup comparisons were not randomized tests of the value of explainability. Explain the named animal readout simply.

title: Inspect Chemical Validity Before Trusting a Pose
bullets: Check stereochemistry, bond geometry and impossible atomic overlaps.
High confidence does not replace those chemical checks.
caption: Illustrative invalid-versus-valid input checks; not results from a named model.
notes: The illustration is explicitly hypothetical. Do not invent measured benchmark results or attribute a synthetic geometry error to a specific software package.

title: Measure Whether AI Improved the Decision
bullets: Count useful hits among compounds actually tested.
Compare with a sensible alternative under comparable conditions.
caption: Hypothetical example: twenty experimentally tested compounds per group.
source: Teaching comparison; no claimed performance for a named model.
notes: The 7/20 and 2/20 counts are invented. They illustrate the denominator and do not establish statistical significance.

title: Exercise: Choose the Next EGFR Experiment
bullets: You have an EGFR structure and a shortlist of candidate inhibitors.
Which tool addresses the pose—and which assay addresses inhibition?
caption: Experimental lapatinib–EGFR complex, PDB 1XKK, as the exercise reference.
source: Wood et al., Cancer Res. 64, 6652–6659 (2004); PDB 1XKK.
notes: A suitable docking/scoring workflow can propose poses; a kinase assay tests inhibition. Discuss receptor conformation and target selectivity. Lapatinib is not presented as AI-discovered.

title: Exercise: What Did an RNA Binding Screen Prove?
bullets: SMRTnet nominated interactions across ten disease-associated RNA targets.
What additional evidence is needed to connect binding to a cellular effect?
caption: Published counts: 190 predicted interactions tested; 40 confirmed by MST.
source: Fei et al., Nat. Biotechnol. (2026), doi:10.1038/s41587-025-02942-z.
notes: Count interactions, not necessarily unique compounds. Binding validation does not alone establish cellular specificity, causality or therapeutic benefit. Ask for a functional experiment and a specificity control.

title: From Target Knowledge to Better PD Decisions
bullets: Define the target interaction or biological effect.
Choose a suitable AI tool, inspect the chemistry and test the claim.
caption: Chemical knowledge makes AI predictions useful—not automatically true.
source: Summary of the cited research examples.
notes: Close the link to enzymes, GPCRs, nuclear receptors, ion channels and nucleic acids. Students should name the question, model output and matching experiment.
